newsitem.title: USA: US pushes emissions trading plan in climate talks.
newsitem.headline: US pushes emissions trading plan in climate talks.

text.p: The Clinton administration proposed a plan Friday that would allow countries to barter allowances for industrial emissions as part of an effort to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
But environmental groups said the pace of the plan was too slow, saying it was full of loopholes.
Under the plan, which was submitted in Geneva ahead of international talks on global climate change, industrialized nations would be held to "budgets" for emissions of heat-trapping gases.
To meet those budgets, countries would be allowed to bank emissions credits or trade them, or implement projects that reduce emissions in developing nations.
The United States still has not proposed numerical targets for emission reductions under the budgets.

Developing countries would not have emissions limits, but would be required to use "no regrets" measures, which U.S. officials described as energy- and money-saving measures such as efficient light bulbs and better insulation.
They also would have to prepare annual inventories of their emissions, and report on steps taken to reduce the emissions that come from burning fossil fuels.
The U.S. plan will be considered along with those of other nations at negotiations to be held in late February and early March in Bonn. The talks are to culminate next December in Kyoto.

In a briefing, Under Secretary of State Tim Wirth said the U.S. plan would give countries flexibility to live within their emissions budgets, and take advantage of improvements in technology as they come along.
"This has to be workable and it has to be achievable. If you set unreasonable targets and goals, that's the fastest way to kill it," Wirth said of the potential international deal.
But environmentalists called it a lame plan that would fail to reduce emissions in time to avert serious consequences of a warming planet.

"Given that there are concrete documented impacts of climate change happening now, this type of proposal from the Clinton administration clearly does not get us to where we need to go," said Kalee Kreider, Climate and Energy Campaign coordinator for Greenpeace.
Dan Becker, director of the Sierra Club's global warming and energy program, said: "It looks designed to gladden the hearts of the nation's worst polluters."
"It basically relies almost entirely on trading and leaky loophole-ridden schemes that will allow polluters to emit pollution now and pay for it later," Becker added.
The Global Climate Coalition, which represents industries opposing strict emissions curbs, called the proposal "very complicated."

"The administration has indicated in the past that it will not cost anything to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Let's wait and ses what the analysis says," coalition executive director John Shlaes said.

The Clinton administration last month proposed making 2010 the first deadline to meet emissions targets. Environmental groups said that was too slow, but administration officials said that was the earliest realistic deadline.

The administration last month also proposed a system in which countries that exceed their emissions allowances could "borrow" against future reductions, a plan most environmental groups derided as passing the buck to the next generation.
But State Department officials said Friday the plan called for imposing penalties for borrowing against future reductions, and said they doubted it would be used very often.
